steps.title: Reporting statements and questions
steps.html:
The backshift. When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, admitted, claimed), the verb inside usually moves one step further back: present simple → past simple, present continuous → past continuous, past simple and present perfect → past perfect, will → would, can → could, must → had to. Forms that are already at the back — past perfect, would, could, should, might — do not move.

When you do not shift. If the reporting verb is present (says, claims, has announced), nothing moves. If the statement is still true or still in the future, shifting is optional: She said the series is nine hours long is fine. In exams, shift unless there is a clear reason not to.

Pronouns, time and place. I → he/she, we → they, my → his/her. Now → then, today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

Questions. A reported question is a statement in shape: no inversion, no do/does/did, no question mark. Why are the answers wrong? → She asked why the answers were wrong. For yes/no questions, add if or whether: Did you see it? → He asked if I had seen it.

Say and tell. Say takes no person, or needs to: she said (that)…, she said to me…. Tell always takes a person: she told me (that)…, never she told that…. That itself can be left out after both.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• She told that she was tired — tell needs a person.
  • He asked me where do I live — no do, no inversion.
  • He asked what is your name? — and no question mark.
  • Forgetting the pronoun shift: He said I was tired when he meant himself.
  • Shifting what cannot shift: He said he had had had…

steps.title: Text A · What the study measured
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Exelmans & Van den Bulck, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 13(8), 2017.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The answer was not the obvious one. The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Ordinary television viewing — switching between a cookery programme with its celebrity chef, a home improvement programme with its DIY tips, whatever is on — showed no such link at all. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. She was careful about the limits, adding that the study was a survey rather than an experiment, so it could not establish which came first.

steps.title: Text B · What the design does
steps.html:
Written for this course.

None of this is accidental on the producers’ side. A drama series is built with a gripping plot broken off at the worst possible moment and the next episode starting by itself, and no commercial break has ever survived contact with that design. Streaming did not invent the cliffhanger; it removed the week that used to follow it. Producers rarely deny this; one has said that the aim is simply to remove every reason to stop, and another has admitted that the design works best on tired people. When a colleague asked me what had actually changed since the days of one episode a week, the honest answer was: the pause.

There is a gap, too, between what people say they watch and what they finish. Asked what they would like more of, viewers almost always mention a current affairs programme or in-depth news, and the same viewers spend the evening with an old sitcom they have already seen twice, playing while they do something else. That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between the viewer somebody intends to be and the one who is tired at half past ten.

The authors’ own recommendation is duller than the headlines it produced. They argued that measures of media exposure ought to take account of how engaged the user is, not merely how long the screen was on, and suggested that anything which reduces arousal before bed would help more than a rule about hours. Whether a habit is addictive, in other words, may depend less on how much of it you consume than on how far into it you go — which is an uncomfortable thought, because engagement is exactly what everybody says they want from television.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
I asked three people how they watched television and what they wished they watched more of. All three said they had very little time. All three, it turned out, had watched something the previous evening.

My sister said she never binge-watched anything, because she fell asleep after twenty minutes. When I asked her what she had seen that week, she admitted that she had finished a six-part drama series in two evenings, and added that this did not count because she had seen it before. My neighbour told me he only watched current affairs programmes and in-depth news. He was not able to name the last one he had watched, and when I asked whether he had a streaming subscription, he said that his son had one and that they sometimes watched a cookery programme together.

The third answer was the honest one. A colleague said she watched three or four episodes back to back most evenings, that the plot was gripping and the format addictive, and that she had stopped pretending otherwise around the age of thirty. She asked me why anybody would lie about it, which I could not answer.

Three people is not a survey, and the pattern still matched the institute’s: what people said they watched described the viewer they intended to be, and only one of them reported the viewer she actually was.
